topics.name: Acts of the Apostles
topics.kicker: New Testament history of the early Church · Pentecost and Paul’s journeys
topics.dates: Usually dated to the late 1st century CE
topics.briefing: In the Acts of the Apostles, the fifth book of the New Testament, a rushing wind fills a room in Jerusalem and tongues of fire rest on Jesus’s followers, who begin speaking in languages they never learned. That scene, called Pentecost, launches the book’s story of the early Church spreading from Jerusalem toward Rome. Its second half follows Paul through riots, prison, and a shipwreck on Malta.
topics.answerHtml: Acts of the Apostles (or Book of Acts; prompt on Luke-Acts)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Parts of this book switch from telling what “they” did to what “we” did, suggesting to many readers that its author traveled with its main missionary. Like an earlier book by the same author, this book is addressed to a man named Theophilus [“thee-OFF-ih-lus”].
tossups.r: Tradition says both books were written by Luke. For 10 points, name this fifth book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: In this book, a young man named Eutychus [“YOO-tih-kus”] falls asleep during a long sermon and drops from a third-story window, but the preacher brings him back to life. Later in this book, that preacher survives a shipwreck on Malta and shakes off a snake that bites his hand.
tossups.r: That preacher, Paul, ends this book under house arrest in Rome. For 10 points, name this New Testament book that comes right after the Gospels.

tossups.p: In this book, the church in Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul on a mission to the island of Cyprus. This book also says that the followers of Jesus were first called “Christians” in Antioch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this book of the Bible that describes the Holy Spirit coming down at Pentecost.

tossups.p: The word “simony” [“SY-muh-nee”], for buying or selling church offices, comes from a magician in this book who offers the apostles money for the power to give people the Holy Spirit. Earlier in this book, a couple named Ananias and Sapphira die suddenly after lying to Peter about money from selling their land.
tossups.r: This book begins with Jesus rising into heaven. For 10 points, name this New Testament book about the early Church.

tossups.p: In this book, a speaker in Athens points to an altar inscribed “To an unknown god” in a speech at the Areopagus [“air-ee-OP-uh-gus”], or Mars Hill. In that speech, he says that in God “we live and move and have our being.”
tossups.r: That speaker, Paul, makes several missionary journeys in this book. For 10 points, name this fifth book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: In this book, a seller of purple cloth named Lydia, often called the first recorded convert in Europe, is baptized at Philippi. Later in Philippi, an earthquake shakes open the doors of a prison where two missionaries have been singing hymns at midnight, and their jailer is baptized.
tossups.r: Those missionaries were Paul and Silas. For 10 points, name this New Testament book that ends with Paul in Rome.

tossups.p: In this book, the evangelist Philip meets a court official of the queen of Ethiopia who is reading the prophet Isaiah while riding in his chariot. Philip explains the passage to him, and the official is baptized in water beside the road.
tossups.r: This book also describes Saul’s conversion on the road to Damascus. For 10 points, name this book that follows the Gospel of John.

tossups.p: In this book, Peter has a vision of a great sheet full of animals that the Law of Moses called unclean, and a voice tells him not to call anything unclean that God has made clean. He then has a Roman centurion named Cornelius [“kor-NEEL-yus”] and his household baptized.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Testament book whose second chapter describes the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

tossups.p: In the fifteenth chapter of this book, a council in Jerusalem decides, on the advice of James, that non-Jewish believers do not have to follow the whole Law of Moses, after Peter, Barnabas, and Paul describe their work among the Gentiles.
tossups.r: This book also tells of Stephen, the first Christian martyr. For 10 points, name this book written by the author of the Gospel of Luke.

tossups.p: In this book, the respected teacher Gamaliel [“guh-MAY-lee-ul”] advises the council called the Sanhedrin [“san-HEE-drin”] to leave the apostles alone, saying that if their movement comes from God, no one will be able to stop it. Paul later says that he studied under Gamaliel.
tossups.r: This book also describes how the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost. For 10 points, name this book that tells the history of the early Church.

tossups.p: Near the start of this book, Peter stands up among about 120 believers, and they cast lots to choose Matthias [“muh-THY-us”] over Joseph Barsabbas [“bar-SAB-us”] to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the Twelve.
tossups.r: This book later follows Paul’s missionary journeys. For 10 points, name this New Testament book written by the author of Luke’s Gospel.

tossups.p: In this book, an angel leads Peter out of prison, and when he knocks at the gate of a house where believers are praying, a servant girl named Rhoda is so overjoyed that she runs inside to tell them without opening the gate.
tossups.r: This book also describes Pentecost and the conversion of Saul. For 10 points, name this New Testament book.

tossups.p: In this book, a silversmith named Demetrius, who made small silver shrines of the goddess Artemis, stirs up a riot in Ephesus, and the crowd shouts “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for about two hours.
tossups.r: The missionary whose preaching angered Demetrius was Paul. For 10 points, name this fifth book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: After a man who had never walked is healed at Lystra [“LISS-truh”] in this book, the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and his companion as Hermes, and the two missionaries tear their clothes to stop the people from offering sacrifices to them.
tossups.r: That companion was Paul, who had been blinded by a light on the road to Damascus. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, one of seven men chosen to hand out food to widows gives a long speech retelling Israel’s history from Abraham to Solomon. The witnesses at that man’s death laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.
tossups.r: That man, Stephen, became the first Christian martyr when a crowd stoned him. For 10 points, name this New Testament book.

clues.t: Fifth book of the New Testament, right after the four Gospels; it tells the history of the early Church
Written by the author of the Gospel of Luke, traditionally Luke the physician
Chapter 2: at Pentecost, the Holy Spirit comes as tongues of fire, and the apostles speak in other languages
Follows Paul’s missionary journeys and ends with him under house arrest in Rome
Saul is blinded by a light on the road to Damascus and becomes a follower of Jesus
Like Luke’s Gospel, it is addressed to a man named Theophilus
Begins with Jesus’s ascension into heaven, forty days after his resurrection
Stephen, one of seven chosen helpers, becomes the first Christian martyr when a crowd stones him
Matthias is chosen by casting lots to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the Twelve
Believers are first called “Christians” at Antioch, whose church sends Barnabas and Saul on a mission to Cyprus
The Council of Jerusalem (chapter 15) rules that non-Jewish believers need not follow the whole Law of Moses
Peter’s vision of a sheet of unclean animals; then the Roman centurion Cornelius is baptized
Ananias and Sapphira die suddenly after lying to Peter about money from a land sale
Its first half centers on Peter, and its second half centers on Paul
The “we” passages, told in the first person plural, suggest that the author traveled with Paul
Simon Magus tries to buy the power to give the Holy Spirit, which gives us the word “simony”
Philip baptizes an Ethiopian court official who was reading Isaiah in his chariot
Paul preaches at the Areopagus (Mars Hill) in Athens about an altar “to an unknown god”
In Philippi, Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, is baptized; an earthquake opens the prison of Paul and Silas, and their jailer is baptized
Eutychus falls asleep during Paul’s long sermon, drops from a third-story window, and is brought back to life
Paul is shipwrecked on Malta and shakes off a viper without harm
An angel frees Peter from prison; the servant girl Rhoda is so excited she forgets to open the gate
Gamaliel, Paul’s teacher, tells the Sanhedrin that if the apostles’ movement is from God, it cannot be stopped
Demetrius the silversmith starts a riot in Ephesus: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
At Lystra, crowds hail Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes
Stephen’s long speech retells Israel’s history from Abraham to Solomon; witnesses laid their cloaks at Saul’s feet

trap.title: The book, not its heroes
trap.body: Most clues follow Peter or Paul, so early buzzers name a person instead of the book. Others hear “by the author of Luke” or “addressed to Theophilus” and answer the Gospel of Luke, the first half of the same two-part work. Paul’s own letters, such as Romans and Galatians, are separate books.
trap.fix: If the question says “this book,” answer “Acts” (or “Acts of the Apostles”). Theophilus plus Jesus’s birth or parables means the Gospel of Luke; Theophilus plus Pentecost, Stephen, or Paul’s journeys means Acts.
trap.line: Real answer line: Acts of the Apostles (or Book of Acts; prompt on Luke-Acts)

topics.name: Judaism
topics.kicker: Monotheistic faith of the Torah · Synagogues, Sabbath, and Talmud
topics.briefing: Judaism is the oldest of the three major Abrahamic religions, which all worship one God. Jews trace their faith to God’s covenant with Abraham and to the Torah, which tradition says Moses received on Mount Sinai. Every week, many Jewish families welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening with candles, blessings over wine and braided challah bread, and a day of rest that lasts until Saturday night.
topics.answerHtml: Judaism (accept Jews or Jewish faith; do not accept “Hebrew” or “Torah”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a Talmud story, a man promised to join this religion if the sage Hillel could teach him its entire law while he stood on one foot. Hillel replied, “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor,” and said that everything else was commentary.
tossups.r: Its followers celebrate Passover and Hanukkah. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers worship in synagogues.

tossups.p: The medieval philosopher Maimonides [“my-MON-ih-deez”] listed this religion’s core beliefs as Thirteen Principles of Faith and wrote the _Guide for the Perplexed_, which tries to bring its teachings into harmony with the philosophy of Aristotle. He also wrote a law code called the _Mishneh Torah_.
tossups.r: This religion’s holiest day is Yom Kippur. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Torah.

tossups.p: Around 200 CE, Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi [“hah-NAH-see”] gathered this religion’s oral laws into the Mishnah [“MISH-nuh”], which is divided into six orders. Later discussions of the Mishnah by rabbis, called the Gemara [“guh-MAR-uh”], were joined to it to form the Talmud.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose followers celebrate Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: A small case called a mezuzah [“meh-ZOO-zuh”], fixed to the doorposts of many homes in this religion, holds a tiny parchment scroll with the Shema [“shuh-MAH”], a prayer that begins “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.”
tossups.r: Its houses of worship are called synagogues. For 10 points, name this religion whose holidays include Passover and Rosh Hashanah.

tossups.p: In the 1700s, Israel ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov [“BAHL shem TOHV”], founded the Hasidic [“huh-SID-ik”] movement in this religion in Eastern Europe, teaching that joyful prayer, song, and sincere devotion matter as much as scholarship.
tossups.r: Its major branches include Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform. For 10 points, name this religion of the Torah.

tossups.p: This religion’s Bible is called the Tanakh [“tah-NAHK”], a name formed from the Hebrew first letters of its three parts: the Law, the Prophets (Nevi’im), and the Writings (Ketuvim). Its books are traditionally counted as 24.
tossups.r: The first part, the Torah, is traditionally said to have been given to Moses on Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Under this religion’s dietary laws, called kashrut [“kahsh-ROOT”], land animals must both chew their cud and have split hooves, and seafood must have both fins and scales, so pork and shellfish are forbidden, and so are many birds of prey.
tossups.r: Followers who keep these laws also separate meat from dairy, and food that follows them is called kosher. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: The _Zohar_, the central book of this religion’s mystical tradition, Kabbalah [“kuh-BAH-luh”], was long credited to the second-century rabbi Simeon bar Yochai [“bar YOH-khye”], but most scholars think Moses de León [“day lay-OHN”] wrote it in 13th-century Spain.
tossups.r: This religion’s teachers are called rabbis. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy texts include the Torah and Talmud.

tossups.p: During the Second Temple period, this religion’s groups included the Sadducees [“SAD-joo-seez”], who accepted only the written law, and the Pharisees [“FAIR-ih-seez”], whose belief in an oral law shaped the rabbis who came after them. A third group, the Essenes, may have written the Dead Sea Scrolls.
tossups.r: Its scripture is the Hebrew Bible. For 10 points, name this religion that grew from the faith of the ancient Israelites.

tossups.p: Karaite [“KAIR-uh-ite”] followers of this religion reject the Talmud and follow only the written Bible. Its Ashkenazi [“ahsh-kuh-NAH-zee”] communities come from Central and Eastern Europe, while its Sephardi [“seh-FAR-dee”] communities trace their roots to Spain and Portugal.
tossups.r: Its followers rest on a weekly day called Shabbat and worship in synagogues. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Public prayer in this religion traditionally requires a minyan [“MIN-yun”], a quorum of ten. When its sacred scroll is read aloud, the reader follows the text with a pointer called a yad [“YAHD”], meaning “hand,” so that the parchment is not touched.
tossups.r: That scroll holds the Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: The philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, a leader of the Haskalah [“hahs-kah-LAH”], or Enlightenment, within this religion, translated the Torah into German in the 1780s. In the early 1800s, its Reform movement began in Germany, holding some services in German instead of Hebrew.
tossups.r: Its other branches include Orthodox and Conservative. For 10 points, name this religion that celebrates Passover and Yom Kippur.

tossups.p: Observant followers of this religion avoid 39 categories of work on their weekly day of rest, and some neighborhoods are surrounded by an eruv [“AIR-uv”], a boundary line that lets people carry things outdoors on that day.
tossups.r: That day of rest, the Sabbath, or Shabbat, lasts from Friday sunset to Saturday night. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: The scholar Rashi [“RAH-shee”], who lived in Troyes [“TRWAH”], France, in the 1000s, wrote line-by-line commentaries on this religion’s Bible and Talmud. Those commentaries are still printed beside the texts in a special typeface named for him.
tossups.r: Its followers celebrate the Sabbath each week and holidays such as Purim and Passover. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Joseph Karo’s 16th-century law code, the _Shulchan Aruch_ [“SHOOL-khahn AH-rookh”], or “Set Table,” became a standard guide to this religion’s practice. At age 13, boys in this religion become a bar mitzvah [“bar MITS-vuh”], or “son of the commandment.”
tossups.r: Many girls celebrate a bat mitzvah at 12 or 13. For 10 points, name this religion whose holy book is the Torah.

clues.t: The oldest of the three major Abrahamic faiths; followers believe God made a covenant with Abraham
Holiest text: the Torah, the five books of Moses, from Genesis to Deuteronomy
Followers worship in synagogues and learn from teachers called rabbis
Holidays include Passover, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hanukkah, and Purim
The Sabbath (Shabbat) lasts from Friday sunset to Saturday night
Symbols include the six-pointed Star of David and the menorah
Its Bible, the Tanakh (24 books), has three parts: Torah (Law), Nevi’im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings)
The Talmud combines the Mishnah (oral law, written down around 200 CE) and the Gemara (later rabbis’ discussions)
The Shema prayer, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one,” is written inside each mezuzah
Kosher dietary laws (kashrut) forbid pork and shellfish and keep meat and dairy apart
At 13, a boy becomes a bar mitzvah (“son of the commandment”); many girls have a bat mitzvah at 12 or 13
Main branches: Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform
Followers believe God gave the Torah to Moses on Mount Sinai; tradition counts 613 commandments (mitzvot) in it
Ashkenazi communities come from Central and Eastern Europe (Yiddish); Sephardi communities from Spain and Portugal (Ladino)
Maimonides wrote the Thirteen Principles of Faith, the _Mishneh Torah_, and the _Guide for the Perplexed_
Asked to teach the whole law while the asker stood on one foot, Hillel said, “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor”; the rest is commentary
Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi compiled the Mishnah, in six orders, around 200 CE
The Baal Shem Tov founded Hasidism in 1700s Eastern Europe, stressing joyful prayer and devotion
Kabbalah, its mystical tradition, centers on the _Zohar_, probably written by Moses de León in 13th-century Spain
Second Temple groups: Sadducees (written law only), Pharisees (oral law), and Essenes (possibly the Dead Sea Scrolls)
Karaites reject the Talmud and follow only the written Bible
Rashi of Troyes, France, wrote famous commentaries on the Bible and Talmud, printed in “Rashi script”
Joseph Karo’s 16th-century law code, the _Shulchan Aruch_ (“Set Table”)
Moses Mendelssohn led the Haskalah (Enlightenment); the Reform movement began in Germany in the early 1800s
Observant followers avoid 39 categories of work on the Sabbath; an eruv boundary lets people carry things outdoors
Public prayer needs a minyan (a quorum of ten); the Torah scroll is read with a pointer called a yad (“hand”)

trap.title: Religion, book, or language?
trap.body: Several near-miss answers circle this one: the Torah is its holiest text, Hebrew is its sacred language, and Israel is both the ancient people’s name and a modern country. None of those is the religion itself. Christianity and Islam also honor Abraham and Moses, so a patriarch or prophet clue alone is not enough.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this religion” or “this faith,” say Judaism (“Jews” or “Jewish” also works). Say Torah only for “this text,” Hebrew only for “this language,” and Talmud only for “this collection” of rabbinic writings. Rabbis, synagogues, kosher laws, and the Shema point to Judaism.
trap.line: Real answer line: Judaism (accept Jews or Jewish faith; do not accept “Hebrew” or “Torah”)

topics.name: Shinto
topics.kicker: Native religion of Japan · Kami spirits, shrines, and torii gates
topics.dates: Ancient · Myths first written down in 712 CE
topics.briefing: Walk through an orange-red torii gate in Japan and you enter a Shinto shrine, a place where people honor kami: spirits believed to dwell in mountains, waterfalls, and ancient trees, in ancestors, and even in great scholars. Shinto has no founder and no single holy book, but its myths, written down in the _Kojiki_ in 712 CE, tell how the sun goddess Amaterasu became the ancestor of Japan’s emperors.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The scholar Motoori Norinaga [“moh-toh-OH-ree noh-ree-NAH-gah”] spent decades writing a commentary on the _Kojiki_ [“KOH-jee-kee”], hoping to recover the beliefs of this religion as they were before Buddhism and Confucianism reached Japan. He belonged to the National Learning, or Kokugaku [“koh-koo-GAH-koo”], movement of the 1700s.
tossups.r: Its spirits are called kami. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, whose shrines are marked by torii gates.

tossups.p: Every 20 years, the main buildings of this religion’s holiest shrine, at Ise [“EE-say”], are rebuilt on a neighboring site using the same ancient methods, a ritual that was held for the 62nd time in 2013. That ritual is called the Shikinen Sengu [“shee-kee-NEN SEN-goo”].
tossups.r: That shrine honors the sun goddess Amaterasu. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In 712 CE, the court official Ō no Yasumaro [“OH noh yah-soo-MAH-roh”] wrote down myths that Hieda no Are [“hee-EH-dah noh AH-reh”] had memorized, producing the _Kojiki_, a key text of this religion. The _Nihon Shoki_ [“nee-HOHN SHOH-kee”] followed in 720.
tossups.r: Those books tell of spirits called kami, such as the sun goddess Amaterasu. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In this religion’s creation story, the divine couple Izanagi [“ee-zah-NAH-gee”] and Izanami [“ee-zah-NAH-mee”] stirred the ocean with a jeweled spear, and the drops that fell from its tip formed the first island. They went on to create the islands of Japan.
tossups.r: The sun goddess Amaterasu was born when Izanagi washed his left eye. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In one myth of this religion, the world went dark when the sun goddess shut herself in a cave, until the goddess Ame-no-Uzume [“AH-meh noh oo-ZOO-meh”] danced on an overturned tub so wildly that the other gods roared with laughter. A mirror hung outside helped draw the sun goddess back out.
tossups.r: That sun goddess, Amaterasu, is honored at the Ise Shrine. For 10 points, name this religion of Japan.

tossups.p: In a myth of this religion, the storm god Susanoo [“soo-SAH-noh-oh”] tricked the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi [“yah-MAH-tah noh oh-ROH-chee”] and slew it, then found the sword Kusanagi [“koo-sah-NAH-gee”] inside one of its tails. Susanoo did this to save a young woman named Kushinada-hime [“koo-shee-NAH-dah HEE-meh”], whom he then married.
tossups.r: That sword became one of Japan’s three Imperial Regalia. For 10 points, name this religion, whose kami include Susanoo’s sister Amaterasu.

tossups.p: In this religion’s myths, the sun goddess gave her grandson Ninigi [“nee-NEE-gee”] a mirror, a sword, and a jewel when she sent him down from heaven to rule Japan. Ninigi’s great-grandson Jimmu was said to be the first emperor.
tossups.r: Those three treasures became the Imperial Regalia. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, which honors kami.

tossups.p: In 1868, Japan’s new Meiji [“MAY-jee”] government ordered this religion’s shrines to be separated from Buddhist temples and later promoted a state form of this religion. After World War II, a 1945 directive from the Allied occupation ended government support for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, whose priests serve spirits called kami.

tossups.p: Students often pray for success on exams at shrines of this religion devoted to Tenjin [“TEN-jin”], the spirit of the scholar Sugawara no Michizane [“soo-gah-WAH-rah noh mee-chee-ZAH-neh”], who came to be honored as a spirit of learning after his death.
tossups.r: Visitors write their wishes on small wooden plaques called ema. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, whose shrines are marked by torii.

tossups.p: Statues of foxes, believed to be messengers of the rice deity Inari [“ee-NAH-ree”], guard many shrines of this religion. The head shrine of Inari, Fushimi Inari [“foo-SHEE-mee ee-NAH-ree”] in Kyoto, sits at the foot of a sacred mountain.
tossups.r: Thousands of bright orange torii gates line the paths up that mountain. For 10 points, name this religion of Japan.

tossups.p: Before approaching a shrine of this religion, visitors rinse their hands and mouth with water from a stone basin, a purification rite called temizu [“teh-MEE-zoo”]. Priests also purify worshippers by waving a wooden wand covered with white paper streamers.
tossups.r: The entrance to such a shrine is marked by a gateway called a torii. For 10 points, name this religion.

tossups.p: Thick ropes of rice straw called shimenawa [“shee-meh-NAH-wah”], often hung with zigzag strips of white paper, mark trees, rocks, and other places that this religion treats as sacred. Sumo wrestlers toss salt into the ring before bouts, a purification ritual with roots in this religion.
tossups.r: Many of those sacred places are believed to be home to spirits called kami. For 10 points, name this religion of Japan.

tossups.p: The shrine of Itsukushima [“ee-tsoo-koo-SHEE-mah”] on the island of Miyajima [“mee-yah-JEE-mah”] is built over the water, so that at high tide it seems to float. Its huge gate, which stands in the sea, is one of Japan’s most famous sights.
tossups.r: That gate is a torii, the symbol of this religion’s shrines. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan.

tossups.p: On the festival of Shichi-Go-San [“shee-chee-goh-SAHN”], or “Seven-Five-Three,” families take children of those ages to shrines of this religion to pray for their health. Millions of people also visit those shrines in the first days of each new year, a custom called hatsumode [“hah-tsoo-MOH-deh”].
tossups.r: Festivals called matsuri often feature portable shrines carried through the streets. For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, which honors spirits called kami.

tossups.p: For centuries, many people in Japan treated this religion’s spirits as local forms of buddhas, an idea called honji suijaku [“HOHN-jee soo-ee-JAH-koo”]. Babies are often blessed at this religion’s shrines, but because it links death with impurity, most funerals in Japan follow Buddhist rites.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this native religion of Japan, centered on shrines and spirits called kami.

clues.t: Native religion of Japan, with no founder and no single holy book
Honors kami: spirits or gods believed to be present in nature, places, ancestors, and great people
Its shrines are marked by torii, gateways that are often painted orange-red
The sun goddess Amaterasu is its most important kami; in myth, Japan’s emperors descend from her
Its name means “way of the gods”
Ise Grand Shrine, its holiest shrine, honors Amaterasu and is rebuilt every 20 years
Key texts: the _Kojiki_ (712) and _Nihon Shoki_ (720), Japan’s oldest books of myths and history
Creator couple Izanagi and Izanami stirred the sea with a jeweled spear to make the first island
Amaterasu hid in a cave and the world went dark until Ame-no-Uzume’s dance and a mirror drew her out
Storm god Susanoo slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi and found the sword Kusanagi in its tail
Three Imperial Regalia: a mirror, a sword (Kusanagi), and a jewel
Purification is central: visitors rinse hands and mouth (temizu) before praying, and priests wave paper-streamer wands
Mixed with Buddhism for centuries until the Meiji government separated them in 1868
Festivals (matsuri) carry portable shrines (mikoshi) through the streets
Motoori Norinaga, a National Learning (Kokugaku) scholar of the 1700s, studied the _Kojiki_ to recover pre-Buddhist beliefs
Ō no Yasumaro wrote the _Kojiki_ from myths memorized by Hieda no Are
Amaterasu’s grandson Ninigi came down to rule Japan; his great-grandson Jimmu was, in myth, the first emperor
A 1945 directive from the Allied occupation ended state support for this faith after World War II
Tenjin, the spirit of the scholar Sugawara no Michizane, is honored for learning; students pray at his shrines before exams
Inari, the kami of rice, uses foxes as messengers; Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari shrine has thousands of torii
Shimenawa (rice-straw ropes) hung with zigzag paper strips mark sacred places
Sumo wrestlers throw salt into the ring to purify it, a ritual rooted in this faith
Itsukushima Shrine on Miyajima seems to float at high tide, and its torii stands in the sea
Shichi-Go-San: children aged 3, 5, and 7 visit shrines; hatsumode is the first shrine visit of the new year
Honji suijaku: the idea that kami are local forms of buddhas
Death is linked with impurity (kegare), so most funerals are Buddhist, while babies are blessed at shrines
Visitors write wishes on wooden plaques called ema

trap.title: Religion or spirits?
trap.body: Shinto clues are full of kami, the spirits it honors, and some tossups ask for the kami themselves, so answering “kami” to a question about the religion (or “Shinto” to a question about the spirits) loses the points. Buddhism is the other trap: most people in Japan take part in both, and shrines and temples often stand side by side.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun: “these spirits” or “these beings” means kami; “this religion” or “this faith” means Shinto (or Shintoism). Shrines, torii, Amaterasu, and the _Kojiki_ mean Shinto; temples, pagodas, Zen, and the Buddha mean Buddhism.

topics.name: Book of Genesis
topics.kicker: First book of the Bible · Creation, Noah, and the patriarchs
topics.briefing: The Bible’s very first words, “In the beginning,” open the Book of Genesis, which runs from the story of creation to the death of Joseph in Egypt. Along the way come some of the most famous stories ever told: Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, Noah’s ark, the Tower of Babel, and the families of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “origin.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On Christmas Eve 1968, astronauts Bill Anders, Jim Lovell, and Frank Borman took turns reading the first ten verses of this book on live television while orbiting the Moon aboard Apollo 8, the first crewed spacecraft to orbit the Moon.
tossups.r: Those verses describe the first days of creation, including God saying “Let there be light.” For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: John Steinbeck took the title of a 1952 novel from a verse in this book, and characters in that novel debate the meaning of a Hebrew word from it, timshel [“TIM-shel”], which they translate as “thou mayest.”
tossups.r: That novel, _East of Eden_, retells this book’s story of Cain and Abel. For 10 points, name this first book of the Torah.

tossups.p: This book says that a river flowing out of a garden split into four branches: the Pishon [“PEE-shon”], the Gihon [“GEE-hon”], the Tigris, and the Euphrates [“yoo-FRAY-teez”]. Cherubim and a flaming sword later guarded the way to that garden’s tree of life.
tossups.r: That garden was Eden, home of Adam and Eve. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: Scholars who follow the documentary hypothesis say this book weaves together older sources, such as the ones they call J and P, which would explain why it seems to tell one story twice, in its first and second chapters.
tossups.r: In those chapters, God creates the world in six days, then forms a man from dust. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: This book is divided into sections by the repeated phrase “These are the generations of,” and it ends with a man dying in Egypt at age 110 after making his brothers promise to carry his bones to Canaan.
tossups.r: That man was Joseph, whose brothers had once sold him. For 10 points, name this first book of the Torah, which begins with creation.

tossups.p: This book says that Enoch “walked with God” and then was gone, because God took him, and that Enoch’s son Methuselah [“meh-THOO-zuh-luh”] lived 969 years, longer than anyone else in the Bible. This book also briefly mentions mighty beings called the Nephilim [“NEF-ih-lim”].
tossups.r: Methuselah’s grandson Noah builds an ark in this book. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: In this book, a man sends out a raven that keeps flying back and forth, then a dove that returns the second time with a freshly plucked olive leaf. His vessel had come to rest on the mountains of Ararat [“AIR-uh-rat”].
tossups.r: God then sets a rainbow in the sky as a sign of his covenant with that man, Noah. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, people settle in the land of Shinar [“SHY-nar”], bake bricks, and use tar for mortar to build a city with a tower reaching toward the heavens, until God confuses their language and scatters them across the earth.
tossups.r: That tower is known as the Tower of Babel. For 10 points, name this book that also tells the story of Noah’s ark.

tossups.p: In this book, a man uses a stone as a pillow and dreams of angels going up and down a stairway to heaven, so he names the place Bethel [“BETH-el”], meaning “house of God.” Years later, after wrestling with a stranger all night, he is renamed Israel.
tossups.r: That man is Jacob, the twin brother of Esau. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: On Ash Wednesday, many Christians receive ashes on their foreheads while hearing words that echo this book: “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” In this book, God makes garments of animal skins for a couple before sending them out of their home.
tossups.r: That couple, Adam and Eve, had eaten fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, a prisoner explains that a ruler’s dream of seven thin cows swallowing seven fat cows means seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and the ruler puts him in charge of storing grain.
tossups.r: That prisoner, Joseph, had been sold into slavery by his brothers. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: In this book, a governor of Egypt has his silver cup hidden in the grain sack of his youngest brother, Benjamin, to test whether his other brothers have changed. Those brothers had once sold the governor to traders for twenty pieces of silver.
tossups.r: That governor, Joseph, is famous for his coat of many colors. For 10 points, name this book.

tossups.p: Michelangelo painted nine scenes from this book down the center of the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512. Those panels begin with _The Separation of Light from Darkness_. Joseph Haydn drew on this book’s opening chapters for a famous oratorio.
tossups.r: The most famous of Michelangelo’s scenes shows God giving life to Adam. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

tossups.p: In this book, two angels urge a man to leave, and he and his family flee to the small town of Zoar [“ZOH-ar”] as burning sulfur rains down on two wicked cities, but his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
tossups.r: Those cities were Sodom and Gomorrah. For 10 points, name this book, which also tells of Abraham and Isaac.

tossups.p: In this book, a hungry hunter sells his birthright to his twin brother for a bowl of red lentil stew, and that brother later wears goatskins on his hands and neck to trick their nearly blind father into blessing him.
tossups.r: Those twins were Esau and Jacob, and Jacob later married the sisters Leah and Rachel. For 10 points, name this first book of the Bible.

clues.t: First book of the Bible, the Torah, and the Old Testament; it has 50 chapters
Opens with God creating the world in six days and resting on the seventh: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth”
Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit in the Garden of Eden and are sent out
Noah builds an ark to survive the Flood
Tells the stories of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of Joseph
Cain kills his brother Abel, then asks God, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”
The Tower of Babel: God confuses the builders’ language and scatters them
After the Flood, God sets a rainbow in the sky as a sign of his covenant; the ark lands on the mountains of Ararat
Esau sells his birthright to his twin, Jacob, for lentil stew; Jacob tricks their father, Isaac, into blessing him
Jacob dreams of a stairway to heaven at Bethel and is renamed Israel after wrestling all night
Joseph, with his coat of many colors, is sold by his brothers, then rises to power in Egypt
Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed; Lot flees to Zoar, but his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt
God tests Abraham, who nearly sacrifices Isaac before an angel stops him
Its Hebrew name is its first word, meaning “in the beginning”; its Greek name means “origin”
Apollo 8’s crew read its first ten verses while orbiting the Moon on Christmas Eve 1968
John Steinbeck’s _East of Eden_ (1952) retells Cain and Abel and debates the Hebrew word timshel, “thou mayest”
A river from Eden splits into four: the Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates; cherubim guard the way to the tree of life
Documentary hypothesis: scholars see older sources such as J and P woven together, giving two creation stories (chapters 1 and 2)
Divided into sections by the repeated phrase “These are the generations of”
Methuselah lives 969 years; his father, Enoch, “walked with God” and was taken; the Nephilim are mentioned
Noah sends out a raven and a dove; the dove returns with a freshly plucked olive leaf
Babel’s builders in the land of Shinar use bricks and tar
Laban tricks Jacob into marrying Leah before Rachel; Jacob works seven more years for Rachel
Joseph explains Pharaoh’s dream of seven fat and seven thin cows: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine
Joseph has a silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack; his brothers had sold him for twenty pieces of silver
Michelangelo painted nine of its scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–1512); Haydn drew on it for his oratorio _The Creation_
Ends with Joseph’s death in Egypt at age 110, after he makes his brothers promise to carry his bones to Canaan
God tells Adam, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” words echoed on Ash Wednesday; God makes garments of skins for the couple

trap.title: First book, not the Torah
trap.body: Genesis is only the first of the five books of the Torah, so answering “Torah,” “Pentateuch,” or “Old Testament” names the whole collection, not this book. Clues about Moses, the burning bush, the ten plagues, and the Red Sea belong to the next book, Exodus, and Joseph’s story, which ends with his family settled in Egypt, is the bridge between them.
trap.fix: Creation, Eden, Cain and Abel, Noah, Babel, Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph mean Genesis; Moses, Pharaoh’s plagues, and Mount Sinai mean Exodus. Say “Genesis” (its Hebrew name, Bereshit, also works).
trap.line: Real answer line: Genesis (or Bereshit; accept First Book of Moses)
